title: Agents are task-based. They should be goal-based.
summary: AI agents execute tasks and stop. The case for goal-based agents that hold a number, a deadline, a budget and boundaries, with the market data behind it.
body_markdown:
*Today's agents execute tasks and stop. A goal-based agent holds an outcome: a number, a deadline, a budget and boundaries, and it works inside those until the number moves. The pieces already exist in shipping products. The task line is where almost every agent product stops, and the market stat below shows what that costs.


Hand a coding agent an issue and it opens a pull request. Hand a support agent a conversation and it replies until a human closes the ticket. The whole agent market works this way: something asks, the agent does, the agent stops. What happens next is always someone else's job.


Even the most goal-flavored feature in a mainstream agent stays inside that shape. Claude Code's /goal command takes a condition and keeps the session working until a separate evaluator says the condition is met. It's the closest thing to an owned outcome I can point at, and the docs (verified November 12, 2026) describe it as a session-scoped shortcut: one goal per session, the evaluator judges the condition against what the agent surfaced in the conversation, and the token spend shows in the status line without a cap.¹ Resume the session mid-goal and the condition carries over while the counters reset. Achieve the goal or clear it and it's gone for good.


So the state of the art is a finish line that lives inside one session. This post is the argument for the level above it: agents should own goals. A goal is a number, a deadline, a budget and boundaries. The agent works inside those, reports progress, and keeps working until the number is met or the budget runs out. Autonomy lives only inside that contract, which is the point. It's scoped and it's verifiable, so you never have to wonder what it's doing with your money.


## What a task-based agent looks like


The pattern is easy to spot once you look for it. GitHub Copilot's coding agent takes an issue and returns a PR, and a human reads the PR to decide whether the work is done.⁷ Intercom's Fin resolves one customer conversation at a time, and its automation rate is a dashboard a human watches; the agent has no target of its own.⁸ Zapier Agents work the same way at the workflow layer: a trigger fires, an execution happens, the execution ends.⁹ Salesforce's Agentforce service agent gets configured with topics, which read more like job descriptions than owned outcomes.¹⁰


Four good products, one shared design: the loop closes through a human. The agent's part starts when asked and ends when delivered. Whatever happens between two runs belongs to the person who configured it. That scoping is what makes these products reliable, and it also caps them at assistant. An assistant is told what done looks like, every single time.


## What goal-based would mean


A goal has four parts, and most agents ship two of them:


- A number that says what done looks like, written so a second process can check it. The Answer.AI researchers who spent a month with Devin put the cost of skipping this precisely: they couldn't predict which tasks would succeed, and the agent would spend days on impossible solutions rather than recognize the blocker.⁵ A checkable finish condition is what lets an agent stop.
- A budget the agent can see and respect. Claude Code's status view shows the current token spend, and that's where it ends.¹ An agent working toward a goal needs the cap in front of it, the same way it sees its instructions. The alternative is you finding out after the invoice.
- Boundaries that survive the session: permissions and scope the agent can't talk its way past mid-run.
- Reporting on a schedule, with progress against the number, so a person can audit it without reading the whole transcript.


Supervision moves from every step to two places: the boundaries and the finish condition. You write them once. The agent operates inside them for the life of the goal.


## The market already voted on this


Sierra has sold outcome-based pricing since December 2024: the customer pays per resolved conversation, and an unresolved conversation costs nothing in most cases.³ Other CX vendors now publish their own versions, and the definitions alone are worth reading. Zendesk's AI agent counts a resolution when the customer doesn't contact again within 72 hours and charges $1.50 for it. Salesforce's Help Agent charges $2.00 when the customer confirms the case was resolved. Intercom's Fin charges $0.99 under its own 24-hour definition.⁴


The same report has the number that should sit with every agent builder. 76% of enterprise CX buyers are open to outcome-based pricing, according to HFS Research. As of July 2026, 5% had contracted on it.⁴ Buyers say they want agents that own a result, then sign on something safer, because the trust isn't there yet. A 15× gap between what the market says it wants and what it buys is the clearest statement of the product gap I know of.


## The famous failures were specification failures


Devin, Cognition's "first AI software engineer", managed 3 successes in 20 tasks when Answer.AI's researchers spent a month with it in early 2025.⁵ Their sharpest line was about the autonomy itself: "Devin would spend days pursuing impossible solutions rather than recognizing fundamental blockers." An agent with no verifiable finish condition has no way to know it's stuck, so it doesn't stop. AutoGPT earned its place in the failure collections the same way, looping on self-verification while the goal it was nominally chasing drifted out of sight.¹¹ 11x reported customer logos and growth it didn't have, which is the third flavor: outcomes claimed without being verifiable.¹² A goal-based system that can't prove its number is indistinguishable from one that made the number up.


The industry's response to all three was to scope everything down to tasks. It fixed the bills and rebuilt some trust, and it also capped the products. Narrow scoping and goal ownership aren't rivals, and Greptile's v5 release shows how they stack. Greptile runs a swarm where each agent explores exactly one hypothesis for a potential bug. The narrow scope made each agent better at its one job: median review time fell from 5:04 to 2:25, and authors now address 66% of Greptile's comments, up from 52%.⁶ The swarm works narrow tasks; the system as a whole holds a standing quality bar that Greptile publishes as numbers.


## What has to exist for goals to work


The pieces are concrete and mostly exist:


1. A finish condition a separate evaluator can check. Claude Code's evaluator reads the conversation and can't run the tests on its own, so the condition has to be provable in the agent's own output.¹ Writing one is its own skill, and it's the same skill as writing evals. (If you want the full method, we wrote one:[how to evaluate an AI agent](https://www.vybe.build/blog/how-to-evaluate-ai-agents) .)
2. A spend cap the agent reads like a constraint, instead of a dashboard the owner checks after the fact.
3. Session-independent state. Goals, budgets and boundaries that persist when the session ends. Cursor moved first here on August 19, 2026: cloud agents got /goal plus event subscriptions, so an agent can hold an objective across check-ins and drive the PRs it opened to completion.² It works inside Cursor's cloud runtime, and the pattern hasn't crossed into a standard yet.
4. Reporting a human can audit on a schedule, with the number in it.


Model capability stopped being the bottleneck some time ago; models are strong enough to hold a narrow outcome. The session boundary is the bottleneck. Almost every agent product still treats the session as the edge of the world, so a goal dies with it or gets carried forward as a stub.


## Where I'd start


We run our agents at Vybe as scheduled tasks, and the ones that hold up over months are rarely the ones with the best model. They're the ones with a number to hit and a boundary not to cross. The rest ask "anything new?" on a timer, whether or not there is anything new, and the answer is usually no. We're working toward goals in the full four-part sense. Right now no one is all the way there, us included.


Open question, and I mean it: what is the smallest outcome you would hand an agent today with a number and a budget attached, and what stops you from writing that contract down?


One concrete thing to try this week: pick the agent you run most, write its finish condition as a single checkable sentence, and put the budget next to it. If the sentence won't come, the agent is running on a recurring prompt, and that's the thing to fix first.
